comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
STATUS UPDATE — `rebar doctor` now exists in core, with its first check. Filed from story affe-2b42-4ee4-4e12 (blocking-link comparability).

MERGE PENDING: this epic and its counterpart both scope `rebar doctor` and overlap substantially. They are now linked `relates_to` so a brainstorm can reconcile them into one canonical epic. That merge is deliberately NOT done here — deciding which survives is the brainstorm's call, which is also why the link is `relates_to` and not `duplicates` (the latter would presuppose the outcome).

WHAT SHIPPED (change 1040, stacked on 1039; both pending review at time of writing):

`rebar doctor [--repair] [--dry-run] [--output json]` — read-only by default, exits 1 while any finding is outstanding so it can gate CI. It began life as a standalone `link-audit` verb; that was rejected for core, because rebar already carries three detect-and-remediate entry points (`fsck --repair`, `validate --fix`, and this) with two different flag names for "fix it". Renamed rather than adding a fourth verb.

Sole check today, named `dependency-graph`: net-active blocking links (`blocks` / `depends_on`) that disagree with the structural comparability rule shipped in 7ab3-9df0-7a90-4ffd. Three finding kinds — `ancestor-blocking` (a ticket blocking its own ancestor/descendant), `mis-escalated` (recorded endpoints differ from what the resolver returns), `unreadable` (an endpoint could not be reduced; reported, never repaired). Classification asks `resolve_hierarchy_link` rather than restating the rule, so the check cannot drift from the resolver it audits.

`--repair` takes no store-wide lock (each write locks itself), refuses to run while a reconciler pass is in flight, and force-writes a `pre-doctor-repair` tag at the pre-run OID as a rollback anchor. It writes a replacement link BEFORE removing the stale one, so an interruption leaves a superset the next run converges rather than losing a dependency. Anything it cannot safely fix — a cyclic or closed-ticket replacement, or a pair whose pair-scoped `unlink` would cancel a different relation — is reported `unrepairable` with the original left intact, and the run continues.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO YET — i.e. what remains this epic's work:
- No check registry. `doctor` hard-codes its one check; there is no `{name, category, run() -> {status, message, fix_command?}, is_required, auto_heal?}` contract, so a second check cannot be added without editing the command.
- No crash isolation and no per-check timeouts. One check raising would abort the run.
- No config, environment, or sync-artifact categories.
- No composition of `validate` / `fsck` / `bridge-fsck`.
- Flag vocabulary is still unreconciled across the three surfaces (`--repair` here and in `fsck`, `--fix` in `validate`).

NEW SCOPE ITEM — re-parenting invalidates the dependency graph. Confirmed empirically, not theorised: the live tracker was remediated to zero scheduling-affecting findings, and within hours two NEW `mis-escalated` edges appeared, both with OPEN endpoints, so they genuinely distorted `ready`/`next-batch`. Comparability is structural, so changing a ticket's parent silently invalidates previously-correct blocking links without touching the links themselves — the store drifts on its own. Per operator direction this is in scope for this epic: re-parent/unparent should either auto-remediate the affected edges when the resolution is unambiguous, or be DENIED with a clear error when it would create an unresolvable situation. That makes `doctor` the backstop rather than the primary defence, and is the strongest argument for the auto-heal category this epic already describes.

Evidence trail for the above lives on 9ad7-d5a2-a664-4827 (the check's implementation ticket): 18 legacy bad edges found on this repository's own tracker, 12 repaired, 8 residual and provably inert (every endpoint closed, so none can appear in ready/next-batch).

comments.body:
Findings from the 2026-08-05/06 codebase-health audit, which ran this epic's premise through its
own verification pipeline. Audit record: `.joe-janitor/report-2026-08-06.md`.

The premise SURVIVED scoring (validity 0.875, impact 0.67) but two of the audit's own sub-claims
were refuted, which changes the shape of the work:

**REFUTED — `fsck` and `validate` do not overlap.** They are cleanly disjoint: `fsck` reads bytes
and git refs (JSON validity, CREATE presence, stale index.lock, SNAPSHOT source_event_uuids,
tracker-vs-origin divergence, forward-compat event types); `validate` reads reduced ticket semantics
(9 hygiene checks plus store-wide HMAC signature integrity). No shared invariant.

**REFUTED — there are not three repair implementations.** There are two, and they are disjoint.
`validate --fix` is a NO-OP: `validate.py:361-362` is literally
`elif arg == "--fix": pass  # accepted, no-op (the bash --fix path is unimplemented)`.
`doctor --repair` and `fsck --repair` repair unrelated defect classes and share only a
`_reconciler_in_flight` probe.

**CONFIRMED and sharper — `doctor` and `validate` DO check the same invariant family.**
`doctor`'s `ancestor-blocking` (`doctor.py:116-119`) maps onto `validate_checks.py:180`
`check_child_parent_deps`; `doctor`'s `mis-escalated` maps onto `validate_checks.py:207`
`check_cross_epic_child_deps`. Not identical — `doctor` covers all ancestor depths but only blocking
relations and all statuses; `validate` covers one hop but any relation and skips closed tickets.
Two implementations, INCOMPATIBLE verdict vocabularies (doctor exits 1; validate scores CRITICAL =
-2), and only one can repair.

**Usage evidence.** `fsck` is load-bearing — invoked by `scripts/probe_rebar.py:513,603`, referenced
by `reconcile-bridge.yml:111`, MCP-exposed, and receiving steady feature work. `validate` is used
but frozen — no behavioural change since the Tier-C port. `doctor` is invoked by NOTHING: two
commits ever (the rename and a Ruff sweep), zero hits across `.github/`, `Makefile`, `scripts/`, and
not on MCP.

**Direction suggested by the evidence.** `fsck` should STAY a distinct verb — load-bearing,
MCP-exposed, actively developed, and the `git fsck` idiom is accurate for byte/ref-level integrity.
`doctor` becomes the umbrella that INVOKES fsck's checks as a category. **`validate` is the actual
consolidation candidate**: its 9 checks become doctor categories, and its two dependency checks
merge with doctor's, resolving the duplicated invariant.

**What breaks, in cost order:** `validate`'s exit contract (0-4 encodes a health score; documented as
a ratified exception in `docs/exit-codes.md` and pinned by `test_exit_codes.py:22`, and this epic's
own AC of "gate on fatal tier only" is INCOMPATIBLE with it — reconcile deliberately); the MCP
surface (`validate()` has a pinned output schema, `doctor` has none); `scripts/probe_rebar.py:421-425`
asserts `validate --output json` emits `score`; and four doc surfaces.

**Cost already incurred by the ambiguity.** Two epics were independently filed for the same command
— this one and `18ae-4f54-a85b-4ddb`, closed as a duplicate. And `docs/chatgpt-agent-guide.md:91`
tells agents to run "`rebar validate` (or `rebar fsck`) to confirm store integrity" — a
wrong-command instruction, since `validate` performs no store-integrity check. No runtime defect has
been traced to the overlap, which is why impact scored moderate rather than high.

**Two cheap wins split out and already filed** under Janitor Cleanup 2026-08-06 as
`7be3-69af-6e84-4235`, so this epic does not need to carry them: removing the advertised-but-absent
`validate --fix`, and correcting the chatgpt-agent-guide line.

**One sequencing note for this epic.** A separate bridge-redesign epic (`2f79-2b32-28c5-4eb3`)
initially proposed a `bridge doctor` verb. It was deliberately deferred to `bridge fsck` instead,
because adding a fourth diagnostic word before the top-level three converge is the failure mode.
Whatever this epic settles on should be the vocabulary the bridge surface adopts later.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
Audit findings from task 7be3-69af-6e84-4235 (the two decoupled wins split out of this consolidation). Recording them here so the consolidation design has the evidence base.

## Capability matrix — the three commands are cleanly disjoint today

| command | reads | checks | can mutate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fsck` | raw event bytes + git refs | store integrity: log/snapshot/ref consistency, orphans | yes (`--repair`, `--dry-run`, `--limit`, `--repair-snapshots`) |
| `validate` | reduced ticket semantics | repo-wide tracker health score 1-5, bucketed critical/major/minor/warning | no |
| `doctor` | link graph + store diagnostics | link/store diagnostic surface, incl. blocking-link audit under older rules | yes (`--repair`, `--dry-run`) |

`fsck` reads bytes; `validate` reads reduced semantics. There is no overlap in what they inspect, so "which one confirms store integrity" has exactly one answer (`fsck`) — which is what made the doc bug below a real misdirection rather than a style nit.

## `validate --fix` was advertised and did nothing

`_engine_support/validate.py` carried `elif arg == "--fix": pass  # accepted, no-op (the bash --fix path is unimplemented)`. It was advertised at SIX independent sites (the in-file `_HELP` usage line and option description, the two runtime "Run with --fix to attempt automatic repairs (interactive)" hints, `_cli/help/validate.txt`, `_cli/help/overview.txt`, `README.md`, and the generated `docs/cli-reference.md`) — and a user following the tool's own printed remedy got silence. Maintainer decision was REMOVE, not implement: `doctor` is the fixing path. Removed under 7be3; `--fix` now falls through validate's existing unknown-option handler (`Unknown option: --fix`, exit 1), and both runtime hints now point at `rebar doctor`.

Note for the consolidation: the under-enumeration of that edit set blocked plan review four times. Any consolidation that moves or renames a flag should treat `grep -rn -- '<flag>' src/ docs/ README.md` as the enumeration method, not a curated list — the generated `docs/cli-reference.md` and the two separate help sources (in-file `_HELP` vs packaged `_cli/help/*.txt`) are easy to miss independently.

## `doctor` is invoked by nothing

`rebar doctor` is dispatched only from `src/rebar/_cli/__init__.py:323`. Outside the CLI dispatch plus its own help text and generated reference, the only mentions in the repo are prose: `CHANGELOG.md` (the entry announcing it) and `docs/ticket-model.md` (two lines describing the blocking-link audit). No script, CI workflow, Makefile target, agent skill, or AGENTS.md/CONTRIBUTING guidance ever tells anyone to run it. So the command the project designates as "the path for fixing" has no adoption surface at all — that gap is arguably more load-bearing for this consolidation than the naming overlap.

## Wrong-command doc, fixed

`docs/chatgpt-agent-guide.md` told agents to run "`rebar validate` (or `rebar fsck`) against the tracker to confirm store integrity". Store integrity is not something `validate` inspects. Corrected under 7be3 to name `fsck`, with a parenthetical stating the split. Prior evidence that this ambiguity costs real work: epics `dabb` and `18ae-4f54-a85b-4ddb` were independently filed scoping the same `doctor` command, and `18ae` was closed as a duplicate.

compiled_state.description:
## Merge note

This epic is the CANONICAL `rebar doctor` epic. It absorbs 18ae-4f54-a85b-4ddb ("rebar doctor command"), which scoped the same command independently and is now closed as a duplicate pointing here. `dabb` survived because it carries the architecture (check registry, crash isolation, per-check timeouts, severity tiers, the exit contract, and the prior-art survey); `18ae` contributed the concrete check inventory and a FIFTH category — sync artifacts — that this epic did not have. Both are preserved below.

## Current status — the command EXISTS, with one check

`rebar doctor [--repair] [--dry-run] [--output json]` shipped from story affe-2b42-4ee4-4e12 (closed). Read-only by default; exits 1 while any finding is outstanding, so it can gate CI.

Its sole check today is `dependency-graph`: net-active blocking links (`blocks`/`depends_on`) that disagree with the structural comparability rule. Three finding kinds — `ancestor-blocking`, `mis-escalated`, `unreadable`. Classification asks `resolve_hierarchy_link` rather than restating the rule, so the check cannot drift from what it audits. `--repair` takes no store-wide lock (each write locks itself), refuses to run while a reconciler pass is in flight, force-writes a `pre-doctor-repair` rollback tag, and writes a replacement link BEFORE removing the stale one so an interruption leaves a superset the next run converges. It began as a standalone `link-audit` verb; that was rejected for core because rebar already had three detect-and-remediate entry points with two different "fix it" flag names, so it became doctor's first check instead.

What does NOT exist yet, i.e. this epic's remaining work: the check registry itself (the one check is hard-coded, so a second cannot be added without editing the command), crash isolation, per-check timeouts, severity tiers, the `--fix`/`--check` flag vocabulary, and every category below except the dependency-graph one.

## Context

Parked from the brainstorm on the migration-pattern epic (odd-vortex-elbow). `rebar
doctor` is a full **diagnose-and-heal health command** in the `brew doctor` /
`flutter doctor` family — a superset of the migration/ensure work. It **depends on**
that migration epic: the ensure-registry + version-marker built there become
doctor's auto-heal category. Design it properly once the migration mechanism exists.

Purpose (per the requesting session): diagnose mismatches between observed project
state and the reported migration version/state; re-apply migrations / correct
inconsistencies that can be **reliably** auto-healed; verify config consistency, that
the ticket store isn't corrupt, and that the environment has the dependencies at the
versions rebar needs; and surface detailed troubleshooting + suggested next steps for
anything it cannot safely auto-heal.

## Proposed design (from OSS research)

**Architecture — a registry of check objects.** Each check:
`{ name, category, run() -> {status, message, fix_command?}, is_required, auto_heal? }`.
Run with **crash-isolation** (one check raising must not abort the run — flutter's
`ValidationResult.crash`) and **per-check timeouts** on anything touching
network/auth. Slow checks run last.

**Four check categories:**
1. **migration / ensure drift** (auto-heal) — the ensure-registry from the migration
   epic; observed-state-vs-marker drift; re-applies idempotent ensures. THIS is the
   provably-safe auto-heal class.
2. **store integrity** (report) — reuse fsck's 5 checks (JSON validity, CREATE
   presence, snapshot consistency, orphan events, push-pending). Non-destructive.
3. **config consistency** (advise / selective-heal) — rebar's own config valid +
   coherent; foreign config only flagged, never silently rewritten.
4. **environment & dependencies** (advise) — Python >=3.11, git present, the
   `[agents]` extra + `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (LLM ops), `acli` (live Jira), pre-commit
   hook wired, and the **"stale global build vs repo venv"** foot-gun called out in
   CLAUDE.local.md (`which rebar` resolves to `.venv/bin/rebar`).

**Diagnose-vs-autoheal rule (converged prior art):** auto-heal a finding ONLY if it is
idempotent + reversible + non-destructive + reliably resolves the state; otherwise
print the exact remediation command + docs link and leave it. rebar's ensures satisfy
this by construction; env/config issues generally do not -> advise.

**Severity + exit contract:** adopt chezmoi's tiers `ok / info / warning / error /
failed` (+ a `healed` result for was-broken-now-fixed). **Exit code keys on the fatal
tier only** — warnings never fail the process (this cures brew doctor's most-cited
flaw). Standard: `0` = clean or warnings-only or all-healed; non-zero = a fatal check
remains after healing. Offer `--check`/`--dry-run` (read-only, exit non-zero if
anything is behind/broken — the terraform `fmt -check` CI-gate pattern) and `--json`
for machine output (test the exit contract; don't let `--json` silently force 0, gh's
bug; don't let an auto-heal reset the failure count, eslint's `--fix` bug).

**Relationship to `upgrade`:** likely `upgrade` = doctor scoped to just the
migration/ensure category (apply pending migrations without the full env/config scan),
or a thin alias — decide when designing.

## Gotchas to design against (ranked, from research)
1. Crying wolf / false positives (brew's reputation) -> severity tiers + ignorable
   non-failing warnings + a per-finding "why this might be fine" note.
2. Wrong exit-code contract (gh#8845 exit-0-on-fail; brew exit-1-on-warning; eslint
   autofix resets exit) -> decide it explicitly and TEST it; gate on fatal only.
3. Network/auth checks that hang (flutter license/proxy; npm ping) -> timeout every
   one; classify timeout distinctly from broken; make them skippable.
4. Non-idempotent/destructive auto-fixes (git `gc --prune=now`; docker `prune -a`)
   -> only auto-heal the safe class; rescue-before-delete; default to report/dry-run.
5. "Fix" that only prints links (RN `--fix`) -> don't market advise-only as autofix.
6. Prerequisite/ordering cascades (docker DDxxxx) -> short-circuit dependents on a
   failed root check instead of emitting a confusing cascade.

Prior art surveyed: brew doctor, flutter doctor, react-native doctor (richest
per-check autofix model — `HealthCheckInterface` with `getDiagnostics` +
`runAutomaticFix`), npm doctor, yarn doctor, gh auth status, rustup (cautionary — no
doctor exists), docker diagnose, git fsck vs git maintenance (sharpest report-vs-mutate
line), terraform validate/fmt, chezmoi doctor (best severity vocabulary).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `rebar doctor` runs a registry of category-tagged checks with crash-isolation and per-check timeouts
- [ ] Auto-heals only the provably-safe class (the migration ensure-registry); advises everything else with an exact next-step command
- [ ] Severity tiers (ok/info/warning/error/failed + healed); exit code gates on the fatal tier only; warnings never fail; behavior is tested
- [ ] `--check`/`--dry-run` read-only mode (CI gate) and `--json` machine output, both with a tested exit-code contract
- [ ] All four categories covered: migration drift (auto-heal), store integrity (reuse fsck), config consistency, environment/dependencies
- [ ] Resolve `upgrade` command relationship (alias vs migration-only subset)
- [ ] Depends on the migration-pattern epic (ensure-registry + version marker) as the auto-heal substrate
## Absorbed from 18ae — the concrete check inventory

The problem 18ae framed: rebar has several independent read-only diagnostic surfaces — `validate` (repo-wide tracker health), `fsck` (event/store integrity), `bridge-fsck` (Jira bridge mapping audit), and the local-dev-env manual checks — each catching a different failure class, with no single entry point. A user hitting a symptom (a claim silently not gated, a stale cache serving old state, a missing venv) has to already know which tool to reach for.

Concrete checks to implement, by category:

1. **Configuration** — config keys unrecognized by the running build (the "unknown key ignored" symptom), missing/misconfigured `rebar.toml` values, conflicting gate settings (e.g. both `require_signature_for_close` and `require_completion_verification_for_close` enabled).
2. **Environment** — a global/stale `rebar` shadowing the repo checkout's venv build, a missing or unwired pre-commit hook (`make hooks` not run), a missing `commit-msg` hook in a fresh worktree, a missing `[agents]` extra when LLM ops are on, missing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`JIRA_API_TOKEN` when their features are enabled.
3. **Ticket data** — wrap/extend `validate` and `fsck` findings (orphaned tickets, cycles, unknown event types from a newer store, stale reducer caches from a mixed-build checkout, malformed attestations) into one report.
4. **Sync artifacts** — NOT in this epic's original four categories. Wrap `bridge-fsck` (orphaned/duplicate/stale Jira bindings) and surface `PUSH_PENDING` (local `tickets` branch ahead of `sync.remote`) plus bridge probe failures.
5. **Dependency graph** — SHIPPED (above).

18ae's auto-repair rule, consistent with this epic's diagnose-vs-autoheal line: restrict it to unambiguous, reversible actions (re-running `make hooks`, clearing a stale reducer cache, pushing a `PUSH_PENDING` branch) and never destructive or ambiguous ones (never silently rewrite ticket events, resolve bridge duplicates, or change `rebar.toml` values without confirmation).

## In-scope follow-ups carried in from story affe-2b42-4ee4-4e12

1. **Re-parenting silently invalidates the dependency graph.** Comparability is structural, so changing a ticket's parent invalidates previously-correct blocking links without touching the links themselves — the store drifts on its own. Confirmed empirically: after remediating this repository's tracker to zero scheduling-affecting findings, two NEW `mis-escalated` edges with OPEN endpoints appeared within hours. Per operator direction: re-parent/unparent should either auto-remediate the affected edges when the resolution is unambiguous, or be DENIED with a clear error when it would create an unresolvable situation. That makes doctor the backstop, not the primary defence.

2. **Escalation is silent on the library and MCP paths.** `add_dependency` prints a machine-readable redirect record to stdout, which the CLI surfaces — but `rebar.link()` calls `composer.link_core(..., quiet=True)` (`src/rebar/_lib_writes.py:615`), and `quiet` redirects stdout/stderr into a `StringIO` sink (`src/rebar/_commands/composer.py:628`), so library and MCP callers have it discarded. That is the same silent-substitution complaint bug 1803-df54-18bb-4881 filed, still present on the path agents actually use. NOTE the fix is not to remove `quiet`: `rebar-mcp` speaks MCP-over-stdio, so an unsuppressed `print()` would inject a bare JSON object into the JSON-RPC stream and corrupt the protocol. The redirect record needs to become a RETURN VALUE threaded through `add_dependency` -> `link_core` -> `rebar.link()` -> the MCP tool result, with the CLI keeping its stdout print.
